processing: Made like other Wuyi rock teas: oxidised, twisted into strips and charcoal or electric roasted. The name fixes the plant and place, not a roast level.
harvest_season: Spring, as with other Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_dry: Dark, twisted strips, as with other Rou Gui.
appearance_wet: Dark leaves with reddened edges, typical of Wuyi Rou Gui.
taste_profile: Sellers describe cinnamon spice and a mineral, lingering finish, which is also the general Rou Gui direction.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, short steeps. Rou Gui can turn sharp if left long.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year, usually after roasting and some rest, like other Wuyi Rou Gui. Place names are easily borrowed, so buy from someone who can say who grew it.
description:
Ma Tou Yan, Horse Head Crag, is one of the Wuyi place names that Rou Gui drinkers look for. Sellers class it with the zheng yan, the true rock tea area, and the trade nickname is Ma Rou, horse meat.

The plant is Rou Gui and the making is ordinary Wuyi rock tea craft, so differences from other Rou Gui come from the ground and the maker. Roast levels vary widely between lots.

Expect cinnamon spice with a mineral finish. Use boiling water and short steeps, and watch for sharpness if you leave it too long.

This is often sold alongside Niu Lan Keng as a name to compare, and doing that side by side is a good lesson. Even experienced makers admit they cannot reliably tell Wuyi places apart by taste, so the seller matters as much as the label.
history:
Little is documented about when Ma Tou Yan Rou Gui became a named tea. The animal-meat nicknames for Rou Gui by place are recent trade language.

Reporting on Wuyi has described companies pushing further names in the same pattern to suggest rarity, which is worth remembering when reading any of these labels.
